title: Maximum Prime Difference
statement:
You get an integer array `nums` that holds at least one prime number. Choose two indices `i` and `j` (they may be the same index) such that `nums[i]` and `nums[j]` are both prime, and return the largest possible value of `|i - j|`.

A prime is an integer greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself, so `1` is not prime. When only one element is prime, the answer is `0`.
constraints: nums contains at least one prime number
notes:
## Intuition

The widest gap between two prime positions always uses the leftmost prime and the rightmost prime: any other pair sits inside that span. So the whole task reduces to "where is the first prime, and where is the last one?" Comparing every pair of primes would also work, but costs O(n²).

Values never exceed 100, so a tiny sieve of Eratosthenes answers "is this prime?" in constant time.

## Approach

1. Build `isPrime` for 0..100: mark 0 and 1 as not prime, then for each prime `p` with `p * p <= 100` cross out `p * p, p * p + p, ...`.
2. Walk `first` from the left until `nums[first]` is prime.
3. Walk `last` from the right until `nums[last]` is prime.
4. Return `last - first`. If there is only one prime, both walks stop on it and the result is 0.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [4, 2, 9, 5, 3]`. The sieve says 4 and 9 are not prime, while 2, 5 and 3 are. From the left, index 0 holds 4 (skip) and index 1 holds 2, so `first = 1`. From the right, index 4 holds 3, which is prime, so `last = 4`. The answer is `4 - 1 = 3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + L log log L) with L = 100: the sieve is a constant-size precomputation and each index is visited at most once by the two walks.
- Space: O(L) for the sieve, which is constant.

## Pitfalls

- `1` is not prime; forgetting `isPrime[1] = false` breaks arrays like `[1, 1, 7]`.
- The two indices may be the same, so a single prime gives `0`, not an error.
- The walks need no bounds check only because a prime is guaranteed to exist.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `limit` | largest value that can appear (100) |
| `isPrime` | sieve: `isPrime[v]` is true when `v` is prime |
| `p` | current sieving prime |
| `multiple` | a multiple of `p` being crossed out |
| `first` | index of the leftmost prime |
| `last` | index of the rightmost prime |

narration.2: Values never exceed 100, so the sieve only needs to cover 0 to 100.
narration.3: Start by assuming every number is prime; the sieve will cross out the rest.
narration.5: 0 and 1 are not prime, so mark them by hand.
narration.6: Sieve with every p whose square is still within the limit.
narration.7: A number already crossed out is composite and its multiples are already handled.
narration.10: Cross out the multiples of p, starting at p * p since smaller ones were crossed out by smaller primes.
narration.15: Begin the search for the leftmost prime at index 0.
narration.16: Keep stepping right while the current value is not prime; a prime is guaranteed to stop the walk.
narration.19: Begin the search for the rightmost prime at the last index.
narration.20: Keep stepping left while the current value is not prime.
narration.23: The leftmost and rightmost primes are the farthest apart, so their index gap is the answer.
